s: Standing.
Standing asks whether this plaintiff is the proper party to bring this claim.
The "irreducible constitutional minimum," as framed in Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife (1992), has three elements.
Injury in fact.
The harm must be concrete, particularized, and actual or imminent.
Concrete means real, not abstract; intangible harms qualify if they bear a close relationship to harms traditionally recognized at common law (Spokeo; TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 2021).
A bare statutory violation is not enough.
Particularized means it affects the plaintiff in a personal and individual way.
Future injury must be "certainly impending" or present a "substantial risk" (Clapper; Susan B. Anthony List).
Causation (traceability).
The injury must be fairly traceable to the defendant's challenged conduct, not the independent action of a third party not before the court.
Standing is hardest to establish when the harm runs through third parties' choices (Murthy v. Missouri, 2024; FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, 2024).
Redressability.
A favorable decision must be likely, not merely speculative, to redress the injury.
Prudential and related limits.

Third-party standing is generally barred, but allowed where the litigant has a close relationship with the right-holder and there is a hindrance to the right-holder's own suit (e.g., doctors for patients; vendors for customers, Craig v. Boren).
Generalized grievances shared by all citizens (e.g., an interest in lawful government) are not cognizable.

Taxpayer standing exists only under the narrow Flast v. Cohen exception for Establishment Clause challenges to congressional spending, which Hein (2007) and Arizona Christian School Tuition Org. v. Winn (2011) confined.
Zone of interests asks whether a statutory claim falls within the interests the statute protects.
Lexmark (2014) recast this as a question of statutory interpretation.
Organizational standing exists either for injury to the organization itself or as associational standing on behalf of members.
State standing includes sovereign, quasi-sovereign and proprietary interests (Massachusetts v. EPA, 2007, "special solicitude"; compare United States v. Texas, 2023, and Biden v. Nebraska, 2023).
Standing is assessed plaintiff by plaintiff, claim by claim, and form of relief by form of relief (Lyons: a past injury supports damages but not an injunction absent a real threat of repetition).
Constitutional standing (Lujan).
Injury in fact: concrete, particularized, actual or imminent.
Causation: fairly traceable to the defendant's challenged conduct.
Redressability: likely to be redressed by a favorable decision.
Check the prudential overlays: third-party standing, generalized grievance, zone of interests.
Repeat for each claim and each form of relief sought.
